title: Given an array of integers that may include negatives and zeros, find the maximum product obtainable from any contiguous non-empty subarray. Solve it with the running max-and-min variant of Kadane's algorithm and demonstrate with a complete banking mini-project.

s1_definition.profdef: The maximum product subarray problem asks for the largest product of any contiguous non-empty subarray of an integer array that may include negative numbers and zeros. It is solved with a linear-pass variant of Kadane's algorithm that tracks both the maximum and the minimum product ending at each position, because a negative element can turn the smallest product into the largest when multiplied, and a zero resets both running products.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, Rajesh looks at a sequence of daily portfolio growth multipliers, where 1.1 means a ten percent gain, 0.9 means a ten percent loss, and a negative multiplier models a reversed position. He wants the most profitable continuous stretch when the daily multipliers are chained together. Because two bad days can multiply into a great result, he has to remember both his best running product and his worst running product each day, since a sudden negative can flip the worst into the best.
s1_definition.oneliner: Track both the running maximum and running minimum product, because a negative flips them, and a zero resets both.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The maximum product subarray problem asks for the largest product of any contiguous non-empty subarray of an integer array that may include negative numbers and zeros. It is solved with a linear-pass variant of Kadane's algorithm that tracks both the maximum and the minimum product ending at each position, because a negative element can turn the smallest product into the largest when multiplied, and a zero resets both running products.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, Rajesh looks at a sequence of daily portfolio growth multipliers, where 1.1 means a ten percent gain, 0.9 means a ten percent loss, and a negative multiplier models a reversed position. He wants the most profitable continuous stretch when the daily multipliers are chained together. Because two bad days can multiply into a great result, he has to remember both his best running product and his worst running product each day, since a sudden negative can flip the worst into the best.

**One line to remember:** Track both the running maximum and running minimum product, because a negative flips them, and a zero resets both.

sections.s2_technical:
Unlike the sum version, products have a twist that forces us to carry two running values. When we multiply by a negative number, the largest product so far becomes the smallest and the smallest becomes the largest. So keeping only a running maximum is not enough, because the real champion might be hiding in a very negative running minimum that a later negative element flips into a large positive. We therefore maintain, at each index, both the maximum product and the minimum product of a subarray ending there.

For each element we must consider three candidates for the new running maximum: the element alone, the element times the previous running maximum, and the element times the previous running minimum. The new running maximum is the largest of these three, and the new running minimum is the smallest of the same three. In code this is `long candMax = Math.max(nums[i], Math.max(prevMax * nums[i], prevMin * nums[i]));` and similarly with `Math.min` for the new minimum. We must compute both using the previous values before overwriting either, which is why we snapshot the previous maximum and minimum first.

A clean way to handle the negative flip without the three-way comparison is to swap the running maximum and minimum whenever the current element is negative, then update each with the element alone or the running value times the element. Zeros are handled naturally because multiplying by zero makes both running products zero, and the next element simply restarts from itself as the larger or smaller candidate. The senior-level nuance is exactly this dual-tracking of maximum and minimum, which is the single idea that separates the product problem from the sum problem.

After updating the two running products at each index, we refresh a global maximum with the current running maximum. The time complexity is linear, O(n), a single pass with a constant amount of work per element, and the space complexity is O(1), just a few scalars. This max-and-min variant is the expected solution and testing it on arrays containing a negative count that is odd, pairs of negatives, and embedded zeros is how you prove it correct.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At the National Bank of India, the wealth-management desk models a client's portfolio as a sequence of daily growth multipliers scaled to integers for exact arithmetic, where values above the base mean a gain, below mean a loss, and a negative models a reversed or short position. The desk wants the most profitable continuous stretch when those daily multipliers are compounded, because that best stretch is used to showcase strategy performance. This is exactly the maximum product subarray problem, complicated by negative multipliers that can flip a losing streak into a winning one.

Problem 2 — Trying every possible stretch by recomputing products from scratch is quadratic and does not scale across the desk's many portfolios and long histories. The max-and-min variant of Kadane's algorithm gives a single linear pass per portfolio, correctly accounting for negative flips and zero resets, which makes the nightly performance computation feasible.

The code has the shared `Account` class, a `PortfolioGrowthAnalyzer` service with a `bestCompoundedStretch` method implementing the dual-tracking algorithm, and a runnable `MaxProductSubarrayDemo` main class that runs Rajesh's and Priya's multiplier sequences, logging each negative flip at fine level and the best product at info level. Integer multipliers are used in the demo for exact arithmetic, noting that production scales to BigDecimal.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: Rajesh's multipliers are 2, 3, -2, 4. We seed the running maximum, running minimum, and global maximum all at the first element, 2.

Step 1 at index 1, value 3: it is not negative, so no swap. New running maximum is the larger of 3 and 2 times 3 which is 6, so running maximum becomes 6. New running minimum is the smaller of 3 and 2 times 3, so running minimum becomes 3. Global maximum becomes 6.

Step 2 at index 2, value -2: it is negative, so we swap, running maximum becomes the old minimum 3 and running minimum becomes the old maximum 6. Now update: new running maximum is the larger of -2 and 3 times -2 which is -6, so running maximum becomes -2. New running minimum is the smaller of -2 and 6 times -2 which is -12, so running minimum becomes -12. Global maximum stays 6.

Step 3 at index 3, value 4: not negative, no swap. New running maximum is the larger of 4 and -2 times 4 which is -8, so running maximum becomes 4. New running minimum is the smaller of 4 and -12 times 4 which is -48, so running minimum becomes -48. Global maximum stays 6.

The best compounded stretch for Rajesh is 6, from the subarray 2 times 3.

sections.s6_takeaway:
The maximum product subarray problem asks for the largest product of any contiguous non-empty subarray of an array that can include negatives and zeros, and I solve it with a linear-pass variant of Kadane's algorithm. The crucial difference from the sum version is that products flip under multiplication by a negative, so the smallest running product can suddenly become the largest. To handle that I carry two running values at each position, the maximum product and the minimum product of a subarray ending there, because the future champion might currently be hiding in a very negative minimum.

At each element I consider the element alone, the element times the previous running maximum, and the element times the previous running minimum, taking the largest of the three as the new running maximum and the smallest as the new running minimum, computing both from the previous values before overwriting either. A tidy way to express the flip is to swap the running maximum and minimum whenever the current element is negative and then update each. Zeros take care of themselves, because multiplying by zero collapses both running products and the next element simply restarts the subarray.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this on the wealth-management desk. We modeled a client's portfolio as a sequence of daily growth multipliers, where some days were gains, some were losses, and a negative modeled a reversed position, and we wanted the most profitable continuous stretch when those multipliers compounded. Because negative multipliers could flip a losing streak into a winning one, the dual max-and-min tracking was essential, and the single linear pass scaled across the desk's many portfolios in the nightly performance run.

The senior-level point I make is that tracking both the maximum and the minimum is the one idea that separates the product problem from the sum problem, and being able to explain why a negative forces that dual state shows I understand the structure rather than pattern-matching. I also mention that products overflow quickly, so in production I accumulate in a wider type or in BigDecimal and I test deliberately against odd counts of negatives, paired negatives, and embedded zeros, which are the three cases where naive solutions break. Naming those exact edge cases and the overflow safeguard is what convinces an interviewer I have solved this carefully in real code.
